name: French Essentials
author: Recurse
subject: languages
description: Greetings, tu vs vous, articles, être and avoir, -er verbs, negation, numbers and questions.

lesson.intro: French is spoken by more than 300 million people across Europe, Africa, Canada and beyond. This pack covers what a first conversation needs: polite greetings, choosing between tu and vous, articles and gender, the verbs être and avoir, regular -er verbs, negation, numbers and questions.

sections.title: Greetings and tu vs vous
sections.body:
In France you greet people before anything else, even when buying bread:

- Bonjour: hello, good morning (used all day)
- Bonsoir: good evening
- Salut: hi or bye, with friends only
- Au revoir: goodbye
- À bientôt: see you soon

French has two words for "you". Use tu with one friend, family member, child or classmate. Use vous with a stranger, an older person, anyone in a professional setting, and with any group of two or more people.

The choice changes whole phrases: s'il te plaît and s'il vous plaît both mean please, and Comment vas-tu ? and Comment allez-vous ? both mean How are you? When unsure, use vous: it is never rude.

Other essentials: merci (thank you), de rien (you're welcome), excusez-moi (excuse me), pardon (sorry), oui (yes), non (no).
sections.code:
A : Bonjour, madame. Comment allez-vous ?
B : Très bien, merci. Et vous ?
A : Bien, merci. Je m'appelle Paul.
B : Enchantée. Je m'appelle Claire.
sections.tip: Ça va ? (literally "it goes?") is the everyday casual way to ask how someone is, and Ça va is also the answer.

check.question: You are speaking to two friends at the same time. Which word do you use for "you"?
check.explanation: Vous is also the plural "you", for any group. Tu only ever addresses one person, so two friends together are vous.

sections.title: Articles and gender
sections.body:
Every French noun is masculine or feminine, and the article shows which:

- le (masculine) and la (feminine) mean "the": le livre, la table
- un (masculine) and une (feminine) mean "a": un livre, une table
- les (the) and des (some) are the plural forms for both genders: les livres, des tables

Before a vowel or a silent h, le and la both shorten to l': l'ami, l'école, l'homme. Dropping a vowel like this is called elision, and it also turns je into j' (j'aime).

The spelling of a noun rarely tells you its gender, so learn every noun with its article. A few patterns help: nouns ending in -tion are feminine (la nation), and most nouns ending in -age are masculine (le fromage, le voyage), with exceptions such as la page and la plage.

Adjectives match the noun: un petit chat, une petite maison. Plurals usually add an -s that is not pronounced, so the article is often the only spoken clue: le livre and les livres differ only in le versus les.
sections.code:
masculine    feminine
the              le livre     la table
a                un livre     une table
the (plural)     les livres   les tables
some (plural)    des livres   des tables
before a vowel   l'ami        l'école

check.question: École (school) is feminine. Which is correct for 'the school'?
check.explanation: École starts with a vowel, so la shortens to l': l'école. La école is never written, even though école is feminine.

sections.title: Être and avoir
sections.body:
Être (to be) and avoir (to have) are the two most important French verbs. Both are irregular, so learn them by heart.

Use être for identity, nationality, profession, description and location:

- Je suis étudiant. (I am a student; no article before the job)
- Elle est canadienne. (She is Canadian.)
- Nous sommes à Paris. (We are in Paris.)

French uses avoir in several places where English uses "to be":

- J'ai vingt ans. (I am twenty; literally I have twenty years)
- J'ai faim. J'ai soif. (I am hungry. I am thirsty.)
- J'ai froid. J'ai chaud. (I am cold. I am hot.)

Note the elision: je ai is always written j'ai.
sections.code:
être     avoir
je / j'      suis     ai
tu           es       as
il, elle     est      a
nous         sommes   avons
vous         êtes     avez
ils, elles   sont     ont
sections.tip: Ils sont (they are) and ils ont (they have) sound different: sont starts with an s sound, while ils ont links with a z sound (il-z-ont).

check.question: Which form completes the sentence? Vous ___ deux enfants. (You have two children.)
check.explanation: Having children uses avoir, and the vous form is avez. Êtes is the vous form of être, and avons belongs to nous.

sections.title: -er verbs and negation
sections.body:
Most French verbs end in -er, and nearly all of them follow the pattern of parler (to speak). Drop -er to get the stem parl-, then add the ending for each person.

The endings -e, -es and -ent are silent, so je parle, tu parles and ils parlent all sound the same. Only nous parlons and vous parlez sound different. Before a vowel, je becomes j': j'aime (I like), j'habite (I live).

To make a sentence negative, wrap ne ... pas around the conjugated verb:

- Je parle anglais. → Je ne parle pas anglais.
- Il aime le thé. → Il n'aime pas le thé. (ne becomes n' before a vowel)

In casual speech the ne is often dropped (Je parle pas anglais), but keep it in writing.
sections.code:
je           parle     (silent ending)
tu           parles    (silent ending)
il, elle     parle     (silent ending)
nous         parlons
vous         parlez
ils, elles   parlent   (silent ending)
sections.tip: After pas, un, une and des usually become de: J'ai un chat → Je n'ai pas de chat.

check.question: Which form completes the sentence? Nous ___ à Paris. (habiter, to live)
check.explanation: The nous ending for -er verbs is -ons, so habiter becomes habitons. Habitez is the vous form.

sections.title: Numbers and questions
sections.body:
Numbers up to 16 have their own names: zéro, un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix, onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize. Then come dix-sept (17), dix-huit (18), dix-neuf (19), vingt (20), vingt et un (21), vingt-deux (22), trente (30), quarante (40), cinquante (50) and soixante (60).

From 70, France counts in twenties:

- 70 is soixante-dix (sixty-ten), and 71 is soixante et onze
- 80 is quatre-vingts (four twenties)
- 90 is quatre-vingt-dix (four twenties and ten)

Belgium and Switzerland say septante (70) and nonante (90) instead.

There are three ways to ask a yes or no question, from casual to formal:

- Raise your voice at the end: Tu parles anglais ?
- Put est-ce que in front: Est-ce que tu parles anglais ?
- Swap the verb and the pronoun, joined by a hyphen (inversion): Parlez-vous anglais ?

Question words: qui (who), qu'est-ce que (what), où (where), quand (when), pourquoi (why), comment (how), combien (how much, how many).
sections.code:
Où habites-tu ? J'habite à Lyon.
Quand est-ce que tu arrives ? À huit heures.
Ça coûte combien ? Dix euros.
sections.tip: In France a space goes before ? and !, as in Ça va ? Both spacing styles are understood.

check.question: What number is quatre-vingt-dix?
check.explanation: Quatre-vingt-dix is four twenties plus ten: 80 + 10 = 90. Quatre-vingts on its own is 80.

keyTerms.definition: Informal "you" for one friend, family member, child or classmate.
Formal "you" for strangers, elders and professional settings, and the plural "you" for any group.
Every noun is masculine (le, un) or feminine (la, une); learn each noun with its article.
Dropping a final vowel before a vowel or silent h, marked with an apostrophe: le ami → l'ami, je ai → j'ai.
"To be": je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont.
"To have", also used for age, hunger and thirst: j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont.
The two-part negation wrapped around the conjugated verb: je ne parle pas.
A phrase put in front of a statement to turn it into a yes or no question: Est-ce que tu viens ?

summary: Greet everyone with bonjour; use vous with strangers, elders and groups, and tu with one friend or family member.
Learn every noun with its article (le, la, l', les; un, une, des), because the spelling rarely shows the gender.
Être and avoir are irregular, and French uses avoir for age, hunger and thirst: j'ai vingt ans, j'ai faim.
Regular -er verbs take -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent; wrap ne ... pas around the verb to make it negative.
Ask questions with rising intonation, with est-ce que, or with inversion (Parlez-vous anglais ?).
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain when to use tu and when to use vous, and how the choice changes phrases like 'please' and 'how are you', to a friend about to visit France.

questions.question: Translate into French: Good evening.
questions.explanation: Bonsoir is the greeting from the evening onward. Bonjour covers the rest of the day, and bonne nuit (good night) is only said before going to bed.

questions.question: How do you politely ask someone's name in French?
questions.answer: Comment vous appelez-vous ? Use vous with strangers and in formal settings; with a friend or a child, ask Comment tu t'appelles ?
questions.explanation: The verb is s'appeler (to be called), so the answer is Je m'appelle ... (My name is ...). The formal question puts vous after the verb, joined by a hyphen.

questions.question: You meet your new manager for the first time. Which question fits?
questions.explanation: Comment allez-vous ? uses vous, the polite form for someone you do not know well or who is senior to you. The other three use tu or the casual salut, which would sound too familiar.

questions.question: Translate into French, speaking formally: please.
questions.explanation: S'il vous plaît (literally "if it pleases you") is the vous form. With a friend you would say s'il te plaît.

questions.question: Which is correct for 'the man'?
questions.explanation: Homme starts with a silent h, so le shortens to l': l'homme. Le homme is the tempting mistake, but French drops the vowel of le and la before a vowel sound.

questions.question: Translate into French, with the article: a car.
questions.explanation: Voiture is feminine, so it takes une. Un voiture is a common mistake: the final -e does not reliably show gender, which is why nouns are learned with their article.

questions.question: Which of these nouns is masculine?
questions.explanation: It is le fromage: most nouns ending in -age are masculine. La maison and la table are feminine, and nouns ending in -tion, like la nation, are feminine.

questions.question: Conjugate être (to be) for nous.
questions.explanation: Être is irregular: je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont. Avons is easy to confuse, but it belongs to avoir.

questions.question: Conjugate avoir (to have) for ils.
questions.explanation: Avoir: j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont. Ils ont links with a z sound (il-z-ont), which keeps it apart from ils sont (they are).

questions.question: How do you say 'I am hungry' in French?
questions.explanation: French expresses hunger with avoir: j'ai faim, literally "I have hunger". Je suis faim is a word-for-word copy of English and is wrong.

questions.question: Translate into French: I am twenty years old.
questions.explanation: Age uses avoir + ans: j'ai vingt ans, literally "I have twenty years". Je suis vingt ans is a common mistake, and ans cannot be left out.

questions.question: Conjugate parler (to speak) for vous.
questions.explanation: Drop -er to get parl- and add the vous ending -ez: vous parlez. Parlons is the nous form.

questions.question: Which three forms of parler sound exactly the same?
questions.explanation: The endings -e, -es and -ent are silent, so je parle, tu parles and ils parlent are all pronounced "parl". The -ent of parlent is the usual trap: on verbs it is silent.

questions.question: Make this sentence negative: Je parle anglais.
questions.explanation: Ne goes before the conjugated verb and pas right after it. Je parle pas anglais is common in speech, but written French keeps the ne.

questions.question: Which is the correct negative of 'J'aime le café'?
choices: Je ne aime pas le café
questions.explanation: Ne becomes n' before a vowel, and pas follows the verb directly: je n'aime pas le café. Je ne aime pas forgets the elision, which is required before a vowel.

questions.question: Write the number 70 in French words, as used in France.
questions.explanation: France counts 70 as sixty-ten: soixante-dix. Then 71 is soixante et onze and 72 is soixante-douze. Belgium and Switzerland say septante instead.

questions.question: Translate the question word into French: where?
questions.explanation: Où means where, as in Où habites-tu ? (Where do you live?). Watch the accent: ou without it means "or".

questions.question: Give three ways to ask 'Do you speak English?' in French, from casual to formal.
questions.answer: Tu parles anglais ? (rising voice), Est-ce que tu parles anglais ? (with est-ce que), and Parlez-vous anglais ? (inversion, the most formal).
questions.explanation: Intonation is the most common in conversation, est-ce que works in any situation, and inversion sounds formal or written. Parlez-vous anglais ? is the standard polite question to a stranger.
